atoms.text: Hi Ryan! You know what's funny? I was looking at running shoes online yesterday, and today my social media feeds are full of ads for sports equipment.
Hello Nina! That doesn't surprise me. Companies collect a lot of data about what people do online.

instruction.text: Which aspect of the digital revolution are Nina and Ryan talking about?

atoms.text: Honestly, I don't mind if it makes websites easier to use. The recommendations are often helpful.
I'm not really comfortable with data tracking. Companies build detailed profiles of users from huge sets of data. I think that's an invasion of privacy.

atoms.a: Why does Nina think data tracking can be useful?
b: It makes sure that companies only collect data with users' permission.
It reduces the amount of advertising she sees online.

atoms.a: What is Ryan's main concern about data tracking?

atoms.text: But is it really that serious? I mean, I don't care if they know I'm buying running shoes.

It's not just about your shoes. Data tracking can have serious consequences. For example, data leaks can expose sensitive personal information, such as details about your health or sexual orientation. Even data that has been anonymised can sometimes be used to identify individuals based on information such as their location and date of birth.
Okay, that's scary. If my location can be tracked without my knowledge, it could even make stalking easier. Tech companies should be more transparent about what happens to our data.

atoms.a: What does Ryan say can happen even when data has been anonymised?
b: ++It can still be used to identify individuals.
It can only be accessed by the government.

atoms.a: What does Nina say tech companies should do?

instruction.text: Read the descriptions of risks associated with data tracking. Fill in the title for each description.

atoms.b:
((Re-identification))
A person's anonymised data is combined with other publicly available information, such as dates of birth or postcodes, making it possible to identify them again.

((Price_discrimination))
An online store collects information about a customer's browsing history and charges different prices based on what it thinks the customer can afford.

((Data_leak))
A company suffers a cyberattack, and customers' personal information is published online without their permission.

((Manipulation))
A website makes it much easier to click 'Accept All Cookies' than to reject them. As a result, it can track users' online behaviour across many websites.

((Chilling_effects))
People know that their searches and online activities are being tracked, so they may avoid reading about sensitive political or social issues.
